topics.title: What Cloud Computing Means
topics.description: Understand the basic meaning of cloud computing, how it works at a high level, and the key ideas behind using computing resources through a cloud provider.

sections.title: What is Cloud Computing?
sections.content:
Cloud computing is the delivery of computing resources over the internet instead of requiring an organization to own and maintain all of the physical infrastructure itself.

These resources can include compute, storage, databases, networking, security services, monitoring, messaging, and many other capabilities.

For example, instead of purchasing a physical server and installing an application on it, you can provision a virtual server from AWS and run your application there.

The important idea is that computing resources can be requested, configured, used, and released when they are needed.

```text
Traditional Infrastructure

Company
   |
   +-- Buy Physical Servers
   +-- Install Operating System
   +-- Configure Network
   +-- Maintain Hardware
   +-- Manage Data Center
   |
   +-- Run Application


Cloud Computing

Company
   |
   +-- Cloud Provider
          |
          +-- Compute
          +-- Storage
          +-- Database
          +-- Networking
          +-- Security
          |
          +-- Application
```

The cloud provider manages the underlying physical infrastructure, while the customer manages the resources and applications according to the type of cloud service being used.

sections.title: Why Cloud Computing Exists
sections.content:
Before cloud computing became widely used, organizations generally had to purchase physical servers, networking equipment, storage systems, and other infrastructure before running applications.

This created several challenges. Hardware required upfront investment, infrastructure could take days or weeks to provision, and organizations had to plan capacity for future growth.

Cloud computing changes this model by allowing infrastructure to be provisioned when it is required.

For example, an organization launching a new application may initially need only a small amount of compute capacity. If traffic increases later, additional resources can be provisioned without purchasing another physical server.

This allows teams to focus more on building and operating applications and less on physically managing infrastructure.

sections.title: How Cloud Computing Works
sections.content:
At a high level, a cloud provider operates large data centers containing physical servers, storage systems, networking equipment, and other infrastructure.

Customers interact with this infrastructure through cloud services and management interfaces such as web consoles, APIs, command-line tools, or infrastructure-as-code.

```text
User / Application Team
          |
          v
   Cloud API / Console
          |
          v
   Cloud Provider Platform
          |
    +-----+-----+-----+
    |           |     |
    v           v     v
 Compute     Storage  Database
    |           |     |
    +-----------+-----+
                |
                v
          Application
```

The customer does not normally need to know which physical server is hosting the workload. The cloud platform provides an abstraction over the underlying infrastructure.

Depending on the service, the cloud provider may manage the physical hardware, networking, operating system, runtime, or other infrastructure components.

sections.title: On-Demand Resources
sections.content:
One of the fundamental ideas in cloud computing is on-demand access to resources.

Instead of purchasing hardware before it is needed, a team can provision resources when a workload requires them.

For example, an application might need a server during development, additional capacity during a product launch, and fewer resources during periods of low traffic.

```text
Demand
  ^
  |                 /\
  |                /  \
  |       /\      /    \
  |______/  \____/      \____
  |
  +----------------------------> Time

Cloud resources can be adjusted as workload requirements change.
```

This model is particularly useful for applications whose workloads are variable or difficult to predict.

sections.title: Scalability and Elasticity
sections.content:
Cloud computing makes it easier to increase or decrease resources according to workload requirements.

**Scalability** refers to the ability of a system to handle increased workload by adding resources or increasing capacity.

**Elasticity** goes a step further by allowing resources to be adjusted dynamically as demand changes.

For example, an application receiving 1,000 requests per minute may require fewer resources than the same application receiving 100,000 requests per minute.

A cloud architecture can use services such as load balancing and Auto Scaling to respond to changing demand.

```text
Low Traffic
    |
    v
[Server 1]

        Traffic increases
               |
               v
[Server 1] [Server 2] [Server 3]

        Traffic decreases
               |
               v
[Server 1]
```

Scalability is not automatic simply because an application runs in the cloud. The application architecture and selected services must be designed to support scaling.

sections.title: Cloud Service Models
sections.content:
Cloud computing services can be understood through different levels of responsibility.

The three commonly discussed service models are Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS), Platform as a Service (PaaS), and Software as a Service (SaaS).

**IaaS** provides fundamental infrastructure resources such as virtual machines, networking, and storage. The customer has more control but also more operational responsibility.

**PaaS** provides a higher-level platform where the cloud provider manages more of the underlying infrastructure and runtime environment.

**SaaS** provides a complete software application that users consume without managing the underlying infrastructure.

```text
More Customer Control
        |
        v
      IaaS
        |
      PaaS
        |
      SaaS
        |
        v
More Provider Management
```

The exact responsibilities depend on the service, so these models are best understood as different levels of abstraction and operational responsibility.

sections.title: Deployment Models
sections.content:
Cloud environments can also be described by how infrastructure is owned and operated.

A **public cloud** provides cloud resources through a cloud provider's shared infrastructure model.

A **private cloud** is dedicated to a particular organization and provides greater control over the environment.

A **hybrid cloud** combines cloud infrastructure with other environments, such as an organization's private data center.

```text
Public Cloud
[ Cloud Provider Infrastructure ]

Private Cloud
[ Organization-Dedicated Infrastructure ]

Hybrid Cloud
[ Private Environment ] <----> [ Public Cloud ]
```

Organizations choose a deployment approach based on requirements such as control, compliance, existing infrastructure, connectivity, workload characteristics, and operational needs.

sections.title: Cloud Computing and AWS
sections.content:
AWS provides a large collection of cloud services that can be combined to build complete applications.

For example, a simple web application might use:

- **Amazon EC2** for virtual machine-based compute.
- **Amazon S3** for object storage.
- **Amazon RDS** for a managed relational database.
- **Amazon VPC** for networking and isolation.
- **Elastic Load Balancing** to distribute incoming traffic.
- **Amazon CloudWatch** for monitoring and operational visibility.

A simplified architecture could look like this:

```text
                    Users
                      |
                      v
               Load Balancer
                      |
              +-------+-------+
              |               |
              v               v
           EC2 Instance    EC2 Instance
              |               |
              +-------+-------+
                      |
          +-----------+-----------+
          |                       |
          v                       v
         RDS                     S3
      Database              Object Storage
```

The services can be replaced or extended depending on the application's requirements. Cloud architecture is therefore about selecting and connecting appropriate services rather than using every available cloud service.

sections.title: Shared Responsibility
sections.content:
Cloud computing does not mean that the cloud provider is responsible for everything.

The provider is responsible for the security and operation of the underlying cloud infrastructure, while the customer remains responsible for many aspects of the workloads running on that infrastructure.

The exact division depends on the service being used.

For example, when using a virtual machine service, the provider manages the physical infrastructure, while the customer may be responsible for the operating system, application, configuration, access permissions, and data.

With a more managed service, the provider may manage significantly more of the underlying infrastructure.

```text
Cloud Provider
    |
    +-- Physical Infrastructure
    +-- Data Center
    +-- Core Cloud Infrastructure

Customer
    |
    +-- Application
    +-- Data
    +-- Access Configuration
    +-- Workload Configuration
```

Understanding this division is important because moving an application to the cloud does not automatically make it secure, highly available, or correctly configured.

sections.title: Key Characteristics of Cloud Computing
sections.content:
The main characteristics that help define cloud computing include:

- **On-demand access:** Resources can be provisioned when they are required.
- **Resource pooling:** Cloud providers operate shared pools of computing infrastructure that can serve many customers while maintaining logical isolation.
- **Elasticity:** Capacity can be adjusted as workload requirements change.
- **Measured usage:** Cloud services can measure resource consumption for billing and operational purposes.
- **Network access:** Resources are generally accessed through networks using consoles, APIs, applications, or command-line tools.
- **Automation:** Infrastructure can be provisioned and managed programmatically.
- **Managed services:** Cloud providers offer services where they operate significant portions of the underlying infrastructure.

Together, these characteristics make cloud computing different from simply placing an application on a remote physical server.

topics.shortDescription: Learn the fundamentals of cloud computing and understand its core concepts, service models, deployment models, scalability, and AWS relationship.

topics.title: Moving to AWS
topics.description: Understand what organizations need to consider when moving applications and infrastructure to AWS, including migration planning, workload assessment, migration strategies, dependencies, security, cost, and post-migration operations.

sections.title: What Moving to AWS Means
sections.content:
Moving to AWS means transferring an application's infrastructure, data, workloads, or services from an existing environment into AWS.

The existing environment might be a physical data center, another cloud provider, a hosting provider, or an older application platform.

Moving to AWS does not always mean rebuilding the entire application. Depending on the workload and business requirements, an organization may move an application with minimal changes, modify parts of it, or redesign it to use AWS-native services.

```text
Existing Environment

Application
    |
    +-- Servers
    +-- Database
    +-- Storage
    +-- Network

          |
          | Migration
          v

AWS
    |
    +-- Compute
    +-- Database
    +-- Storage
    +-- Networking
    +-- Security
    +-- Monitoring
```

The goal should be more than simply moving servers. A successful migration should preserve business functionality while meeting requirements for availability, security, performance, operations, and cost.

sections.title: Why Organizations Move to AWS
sections.content:
Organizations move workloads to AWS for different reasons, and the reason for migration should be identified before selecting a migration approach.

Common drivers include:

- Replacing aging physical infrastructure.
- Reducing data-center management responsibilities.
- Increasing infrastructure scalability.
- Improving application availability.
- Expanding applications into new geographic locations.
- Using managed AWS services.
- Improving infrastructure automation.
- Modernizing applications.
- Changing infrastructure spending from large upfront hardware purchases to cloud-based consumption.

The expected business outcome matters because a migration designed only to move servers may not provide the same benefits as a migration that also modernizes the application.

sections.title: Assess the Existing Environment
sections.content:
Before moving a workload to AWS, understand what currently exists.

An assessment should identify the application's servers, databases, storage, network connections, operating systems, dependencies, traffic patterns, security requirements, and operational processes.

For example, an application may appear to run on a single server but actually depend on a database server, file share, DNS configuration, scheduled jobs, external APIs, and internal services.

```text
                 Application
                      |
        +-------------+-------------+
        |             |             |
        v             v             v
     Database      File Store    External API
        |
        v
   Backup System
```

Missing one of these dependencies during migration can cause the application to work in a test environment but fail after production cutover.

A useful assessment therefore focuses on dependencies and actual application behavior, not just the list of servers.

sections.title: Migration Strategies
sections.content:
Different workloads require different migration approaches. A common framework describes six migration strategies: rehost, replatform, repurchase, refactor or re-architect, retire, and retain.

**Rehost** means moving the workload with minimal application changes.

**Replatform** means making limited changes to take advantage of a cloud capability without completely redesigning the application.

**Repurchase** means replacing an existing solution with a different product or service, often using a cloud-based software offering.

**Refactor or re-architect** means significantly changing the application's architecture to take advantage of cloud-native capabilities.

**Retire** means removing applications or components that are no longer needed.

**Retain** means keeping a workload in its existing environment when migration is not currently justified.

```text
Existing Workload
       |
       +-- Minimal change --------> Rehost
       |
       +-- Some optimization ------> Replatform
       |
       +-- Replace product --------> Repurchase
       |
       +-- Redesign architecture --> Refactor
       |
       +-- No longer needed --------> Retire
       |
       +-- Stay where it is --------> Retain
```

The strategy should be selected per workload rather than assuming that every application should use the same migration method.

sections.title: Rehost vs Replatform vs Refactor
sections.content:
These migration approaches differ mainly in how much the application changes during migration.

With **rehosting**, the objective is usually to move the workload quickly with minimal changes. This can be useful when the immediate priority is leaving an existing data center.

With **replatforming**, the application is changed enough to use selected managed capabilities while keeping most of the application architecture intact.

With **refactoring**, the application architecture is redesigned. Components may be split into services, databases may change, and the application may adopt serverless, containers, event-driven processing, or other cloud-native patterns.

```text
Less Application Change
        |
        v
     Rehost
        |
    Replatform
        |
     Refactor
        |
        v
More Application Change
```

More architectural change can provide additional cloud capabilities, but it generally introduces more development, testing, and migration complexity.

sections.title: Plan the Migration
sections.content:
A migration should be treated as a project rather than a simple server move.

A migration plan normally defines the workloads being migrated, dependencies, target AWS services, migration sequence, testing approach, rollback plan, security requirements, data migration approach, and production cutover process.

A useful sequence is:

```text
Discover
   |
   v
Assess
   |
   v
Plan
   |
   v
Design AWS Environment
   |
   v
Migrate / Test
   |
   v
Cut Over
   |
   v
Operate and Optimize
```

Migration waves can also be used. Instead of moving every application simultaneously, related workloads can be grouped and migrated in controlled stages.

sections.title: Understand Application Dependencies
sections.content:
Application dependencies are one of the most important areas to understand before migration.

An application may depend on databases, shared storage, authentication systems, DNS, message queues, monitoring systems, third-party APIs, network connections, or other internal applications.

For example:

```text
Web Application
      |
      +------> Authentication Service
      |
      +------> Database
      |
      +------> Redis Cache
      |
      +------> File Storage
      |
      +------> External Payment API
```

If the application is migrated without considering these dependencies, requests may fail even though the main application server is running correctly.

Dependency mapping also helps determine the order in which workloads should be migrated and whether temporary connectivity between the old and new environments is required.

sections.title: Data Migration
sections.content:
Moving an application to AWS often requires moving its data as well. The appropriate approach depends on the amount of data, database technology, acceptable downtime, network connectivity, and consistency requirements.

For a database migration, the process may involve copying existing data, synchronizing changes, validating the target database, and then switching the application to the new database.

```text
Existing Database
       |
       | Initial Data Copy
       v
AWS Database
       ^
       |
       | Continuous Changes
       |
Existing Database

        Cutover
           |
           v
Application → AWS Database
```

For large datasets, transferring everything over a normal internet connection may not be practical. The migration design should therefore consider transfer time, bandwidth, synchronization, validation, and the final cutover window.

sections.title: Network Connectivity During Migration
sections.content:
During a migration, the existing environment and AWS may need to communicate with each other before the migration is complete.

This can be required when an application component has already moved to AWS while another dependency remains in the existing environment.

```text
Existing Data Center                    AWS
+------------------+              +------------------+
| Application A    |<------------>| Application B    |
| Database         |   Network     | Database         |
| Internal APIs    |   Connection  | Services         |
+------------------+              +------------------+
```

Depending on the environment, connectivity can be established using technologies such as site-to-site VPN or AWS Direct Connect.

The migration network should be designed with routing, security, bandwidth, latency, monitoring, and failure scenarios in mind.

sections.title: Security During Migration
sections.content:
Security should be considered throughout the migration rather than added after the workload has moved.

Before migration, identify sensitive data, required access, network boundaries, encryption requirements, credentials, logging requirements, and compliance constraints.

During migration, access should be limited to the people and systems that actually require it. Data transferred between environments should also be protected appropriately.

After migration, review IAM permissions, security groups, network controls, encryption, logging, monitoring, and credential management.

```text
Migration Security
       |
       +-- Identity and Access
       +-- Network Security
       +-- Encryption
       +-- Data Protection
       +-- Logging
       +-- Monitoring
       +-- Compliance
```

A migration should not create broader access simply because temporary access was convenient during the move.

sections.title: Testing Before Cutover
sections.content:
Before production cutover, the migrated workload should be tested in the AWS environment.

Testing should verify application functionality, database connectivity, integrations, network communication, authentication, performance, monitoring, backups, and failure behavior.

The goal is not only to confirm that the application starts. The important question is whether users can perform the same business operations successfully in the new environment.

```text
Migration Test
      |
      +-- Functional Testing
      +-- Integration Testing
      +-- Performance Testing
      +-- Security Testing
      +-- Data Validation
      +-- Backup / Recovery Testing
      +-- Monitoring Validation
```

For critical applications, a rollback procedure should also be tested or at least validated before the final cutover.

sections.title: Production Cutover
sections.content:
Cutover is the point at which production traffic is directed to the AWS environment.

A cutover plan should define the exact sequence of actions, responsible people, validation checks, communication process, expected downtime if any, and rollback conditions.

A simplified flow is:

```text
Existing Production
        |
        | Final Synchronization
        v
      AWS
        |
   Validation
        |
        v
Update Traffic / DNS
        |
        v
AWS Becomes Production
```

The cutover should be performed during an appropriate maintenance window when possible. After traffic is switched, application health, errors, latency, database behavior, and business transactions should be monitored closely.

sections.title: After Migration
sections.content:
Migration is not complete simply because the application is running in AWS. The environment should be reviewed and optimized after the workload becomes stable.

Post-migration activities can include:

- Monitoring application and infrastructure metrics.
- Reviewing AWS service configuration.
- Removing temporary migration resources.
- Reviewing IAM permissions.
- Validating backups and recovery procedures.
- Optimizing compute and storage resources.
- Reviewing AWS costs.
- Improving automation and deployment processes.
- Documenting the new architecture.

```text
Migration Complete
       |
       v
Monitor
       |
       v
Validate
       |
       v
Optimize
       |
       v
Automate
       |
       v
Continuously Improve
```

This post-migration phase is important because the first AWS design is not necessarily the final optimized design.

topics.shortDescription: Learn how to approach moving existing applications and infrastructure to AWS, from assessment and migration strategy through data migration, testing, cutover, and post-migration optimization.

topics.title: Infrastructure As A Service
topics.description: Understand Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS), what it provides, how responsibility is divided between the cloud provider and customer, and when an IaaS model is useful.

sections.title: What is IaaS?
sections.content:
Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) is a cloud service model that provides fundamental computing infrastructure on demand. Instead of purchasing physical servers, storage devices, and networking equipment, an organization can provision these resources from a cloud provider.

Typical IaaS resources include virtual machines, storage, networking, and related infrastructure capabilities.

```text
              IaaS
               |
      +--------+--------+
      |        |        |
      v        v        v
   Compute   Storage  Networking
      |        |        |
      +--------+--------+
               |
               v
        Customer Workload
```

The customer generally has more control over the operating system, applications, configurations, and data than with higher-level cloud service models.

For example, Amazon EC2 can provide virtual servers where an organization chooses the instance type, operating system, networking configuration, storage, and application software it needs.

sections.title: What IaaS Provides
sections.content:
IaaS focuses on providing the building blocks required to run workloads.

Common capabilities include:

- Virtual machines or compute instances.
- Block and object storage.
- Virtual networks and subnets.
- Network interfaces and routing.
- Firewalls and security controls.
- Load balancing and other infrastructure components.

The exact services depend on the cloud provider, but the basic idea remains the same: the provider supplies the infrastructure, while the customer configures and operates the workload running on it.

sections.title: Shared Responsibility in IaaS
sections.content:
With IaaS, the cloud provider manages the underlying physical infrastructure, while the customer manages a larger portion of the software environment.

```text
Cloud Provider
    |
    +-- Data Center
    +-- Physical Servers
    +-- Physical Storage
    +-- Physical Networking
    +-- Core Infrastructure

Customer
    |
    +-- Operating System
    +-- Applications
    +-- Data
    +-- User Access
    +-- Workload Configuration
```

For example, when running an application on an EC2 instance, AWS manages the physical server and underlying cloud infrastructure. The customer is responsible for the operating system configuration, application, data, and appropriate security configuration.

The exact boundary can vary depending on the AWS service and configuration.

sections.title: When IaaS Makes Sense
sections.content:
IaaS is useful when an organization needs significant control over its computing environment.

Typical situations include:

- Applications that require operating-system-level configuration.
- Legacy applications that cannot easily be redesigned.
- Workloads requiring specific software or runtime configurations.
- Development and testing environments.
- Applications being migrated from physical servers with minimal architectural changes.

The trade-off is that greater control also means greater operational responsibility. The team may need to manage operating system updates, application deployment, monitoring, security configuration, and other operational tasks.

sections.title: IaaS Example on AWS
sections.content:
Consider a Java application that previously ran on a physical Linux server.

A simple migration could use an EC2 instance as the compute layer.

```text
Users
  |
  v
Load Balancer
  |
  v
EC2 Instance
  |
  +---- Java Application
  |
  +---- Operating System
  |
  +---- EBS Storage
```

This approach allows the application team to retain substantial control over the server environment while moving the physical infrastructure responsibility to AWS.

As the architecture evolves, the application could later adopt managed services such as Amazon RDS, Amazon S3, or container platforms.

topics.shortDescription: Learn how IaaS provides on-demand compute, storage, and networking while giving customers significant control over their workloads.

topics.title: Platform As A Service
topics.description: Understand Platform as a Service (PaaS), how it abstracts infrastructure management, and how developers use managed platforms to build and deploy applications.

sections.title: What is PaaS?
sections.content:
Platform as a Service (PaaS) provides a managed application platform on which developers can build, deploy, and run applications without managing all of the underlying infrastructure themselves.

The cloud provider manages more of the infrastructure and platform components compared with IaaS.

```text
IaaS
Customer manages more
        |
        v
Operating System
Runtime
Application

PaaS
Provider manages more
        |
        v
Infrastructure
Operating System
Platform Runtime
        |
        v
Customer focuses mainly on Application
```

The exact responsibility boundary depends on the service, but the main purpose of PaaS is to let development teams focus more on application code and less on infrastructure administration.

sections.title: How PaaS Works
sections.content:
With a PaaS model, the provider supplies an environment where applications can be deployed and executed.

The platform can handle infrastructure tasks such as server provisioning, runtime management, and parts of scaling and deployment depending on the service.

```text
Developer
    |
    | Application Code
    v
   PaaS
    |
    +-- Runtime
    +-- Operating Environment
    +-- Infrastructure
    +-- Scaling / Platform Management
    |
    v
 Cloud Infrastructure
```

Developers typically interact with the platform through deployment tools, APIs, command-line interfaces, or source-control integrations rather than manually configuring every server.

sections.title: Benefits of PaaS
sections.content:
PaaS can reduce the amount of infrastructure work required from application teams.

Common benefits include:

- Faster application deployment.
- Less operating-system and server administration.
- Standardized application environments.
- Easier integration with other managed cloud services.
- Support for automated deployment workflows.
- More time for developers to focus on application functionality.

The trade-off is reduced infrastructure control compared with IaaS. The platform determines or constrains some parts of the runtime environment.

sections.title: PaaS Example on AWS
sections.content:
AWS provides several services that can provide platform-like experiences depending on the workload and configuration. For example, AWS Elastic Beanstalk can simplify deploying applications by handling much of the underlying infrastructure setup.

```text
Developer
    |
    v
Application Code
    |
    v
Elastic Beanstalk
    |
    +-- Compute Environment
    +-- Deployment
    +-- Scaling Configuration
    +-- Monitoring Integration
    |
    v
AWS Infrastructure
```

The developer can concentrate primarily on the application while the platform handles significant portions of the deployment environment.

sections.title: IaaS vs PaaS
sections.content:
The main difference between IaaS and PaaS is the level of abstraction and responsibility.

```text
                 IaaS              PaaS

Application       You               You
Data              You               You
Runtime           You               Provider / Platform
OS                You               Provider / Platform
Infrastructure    Provider          Provider

Control           Higher            Lower
Management        More              Less
```

IaaS provides more control but requires more operational work. PaaS provides a higher-level environment that can reduce infrastructure management but may impose platform constraints.

topics.shortDescription: Learn how PaaS provides a managed application platform and reduces the infrastructure responsibilities handled directly by developers.

topics.title: Software As A Service
topics.description: Understand Software as a Service (SaaS), how users consume complete software applications through the internet, and how SaaS differs from IaaS and PaaS.

sections.title: What is SaaS?
sections.content:
Software as a Service (SaaS) is a cloud service model in which users consume a complete software application managed by the service provider.

The user generally does not manage the underlying servers, operating system, runtime, or application infrastructure. The provider operates the software and makes it available through a network connection, commonly using a web browser or application interface.

```text
User
  |
  v
SaaS Application
  |
  +-- Application Software
  +-- Runtime
  +-- Operating System
  +-- Infrastructure
  |
  v
Cloud Provider
```

Examples of SaaS include online email, collaboration platforms, customer relationship management systems, and other complete software products delivered as a service.

sections.title: How SaaS Works
sections.content:
With SaaS, the provider operates the application and its supporting infrastructure. Users normally access the application without managing the underlying technology stack.

```text
                 Internet
                    |
          +---------+---------+
          |                   |
          v                   v
       User A              User B
          |                   |
          +---------+---------+
                    |
                    v
             SaaS Application
                    |
                    v
            Cloud Infrastructure
```

The provider is responsible for application availability, platform operations, infrastructure, updates, and many other operational tasks, although the exact responsibilities depend on the SaaS product and its terms.

sections.title: Benefits of SaaS
sections.content:
SaaS removes much of the infrastructure and software-management work from the customer.

Common benefits include:

- No need to maintain application servers directly.
- Faster access to a complete application.
- Provider-managed updates and maintenance.
- Access from different devices and locations.
- Easier adoption for standard business functions.
- Reduced need for organizations to operate the underlying software infrastructure.

The trade-off is that customers have less control over the application's underlying implementation and infrastructure.

sections.title: SaaS vs PaaS vs IaaS
sections.content:
The three models differ mainly in how much of the technology stack is managed by the provider.

```text
                IaaS        PaaS        SaaS

Application      You          You        Provider
Data             You          You        Shared / Product
Runtime          You        Provider    Provider
OS               You        Provider    Provider
Infrastructure   Provider   Provider    Provider

Control          High        Medium       Low
Management       More        Less         Least
```

IaaS is closer to raw infrastructure. PaaS provides a managed application platform. SaaS provides a complete application that users consume.

The choice depends on whether the organization needs infrastructure control, development flexibility, or simply wants to consume a finished software product.

sections.title: SaaS in Everyday Computing
sections.content:
Many applications people use every day follow the SaaS model. Users sign in to the application and use its functionality without installing and maintaining the servers that operate the product.

For an organization, using SaaS can mean that an internal team does not need to build and maintain a complete software platform for a common business requirement.

The organization instead focuses on configuring users, permissions, business settings, integrations, and data while the SaaS provider operates the application itself.

topics.shortDescription: Learn how SaaS delivers complete software applications through the cloud and understand its differences from IaaS and PaaS.

topics.title: Essential Cloud Characteristics
topics.description: Learn the fundamental characteristics that distinguish cloud computing from traditional infrastructure, including on-demand access, resource pooling, elasticity, network access, and measured usage.

sections.title: Overview of Cloud Characteristics
sections.content:
Cloud computing is more than hosting an application on a remote server. It has several characteristics that define how cloud resources are provisioned and consumed.

The core characteristics include:

- On-demand self-service.
- Broad network access.
- Resource pooling.
- Rapid elasticity.
- Measured or metered usage.

These characteristics explain why cloud platforms can provide infrastructure differently from traditional physical data centers.

sections.title: On-Demand Self-Service
sections.content:
On-demand self-service means that users can provision computing resources when they need them without requiring someone to manually install physical hardware for every request.

For example, a team can create an EC2 instance through the AWS Management Console, CLI, API, or infrastructure-as-code.

```text
Developer
    |
    v
AWS Console / API / CLI
    |
    v
Provision Resource
    |
    v
EC2 / S3 / RDS / Other Service
```

This allows infrastructure provisioning to become part of an automated development and deployment process.

sections.title: Broad Network Access
sections.content:
Cloud resources are designed to be accessible over networks using standard mechanisms such as web interfaces, APIs, applications, and command-line tools.

For example, an application can communicate with an AWS database over a network, while an administrator can manage cloud resources through an API or console.

Network access also means that security controls are essential. Resources should not automatically be exposed to the public internet simply because they are hosted in the cloud.

sections.title: Resource Pooling
sections.content:
Cloud providers operate large pools of physical computing resources and allocate capacity to customers through cloud services.

Customers generally interact with logical resources rather than selecting a particular physical machine in a data center.

```text
              Cloud Provider
                    |
        +-----------+-----------+
        |           |           |
        v           v           v
    Physical     Physical    Physical
    Servers      Servers     Servers
        \           |           /
         \          |          /
          +---------+---------+
                    |
             Cloud Resources
                    |
          +---------+---------+
          |                   |
          v                   v
       Customer A          Customer B
```

Isolation mechanisms allow different customers and workloads to use shared physical infrastructure while maintaining logical separation.

sections.title: Rapid Elasticity
sections.content:
Rapid elasticity is the ability to adjust resource capacity as workload requirements change.

An application may need additional capacity during a traffic spike and less capacity when demand falls.

```text
Traffic
  ^
  |             /\
  |            /  \
  |      /\   /    \
  |_____/  \_/      \____
  |
  +----------------------> Time

Resources can scale with demand.
```

AWS services such as Auto Scaling can help automate capacity changes for suitable workloads. Elasticity still depends on the architecture and the services being used.

sections.title: Measured Usage
sections.content:
Cloud services can measure resource consumption. This allows usage to be tracked for billing, monitoring, capacity planning, and cost management.

Depending on the service, usage can be associated with factors such as compute time, storage consumed, requests, data transfer, or other service-specific units.

```text
Cloud Resource
      |
      v
Usage Measurement
      |
      +----> Billing
      +----> Monitoring
      +----> Cost Analysis
      +----> Capacity Planning
```

This measured model makes it important to monitor cloud usage rather than assuming that resources are free simply because they can be provisioned easily.

sections.title: Why These Characteristics Matter
sections.content:
The characteristics work together to create the cloud operating model.

For example, on-demand self-service allows a team to create resources, resource pooling allows the provider to operate infrastructure efficiently, network access allows applications and users to interact with services, elasticity allows capacity to change, and measured usage allows consumption to be tracked.

```text
On-Demand
    +
Network Access
    +
Resource Pooling
    +
Elasticity
    +
Measured Usage
    |
    v
Cloud Computing Model
```

Understanding these characteristics helps explain why cloud computing is different from simply renting a physical server.

topics.shortDescription: Understand the core characteristics that make cloud computing different from traditional infrastructure.

topics.title: Operational Benefits
topics.description: Understand the operational benefits cloud computing can provide, including faster provisioning, automation, scalability, managed services, global deployment, monitoring, and improved infrastructure operations.

sections.title: What Operational Benefits Mean
sections.content:
Operational benefits are improvements in how teams build, deploy, manage, monitor, and maintain applications and infrastructure.

Cloud computing can change infrastructure operations from a hardware-focused process into a software-driven process.

```text
Traditional Operations

Request Hardware
      |
      v
Purchase
      |
      v
Install
      |
      v
Configure
      |
      v
Deploy


Cloud Operations

Define Resource
      |
      v
Provision through API / IaC
      |
      v
Configure
      |
      v
Deploy
      |
      v
Monitor / Automate
```

The benefits depend on how the organization uses cloud capabilities. Simply moving an existing application to a cloud provider does not automatically provide every operational benefit.

sections.title: Faster Provisioning
sections.content:
Cloud resources can generally be provisioned much faster than purchasing and installing physical infrastructure.

A development team can create a test environment when required and configure it using automation.

```text
Requirement
    |
    v
Infrastructure Definition
    |
    v
Cloud API / IaC
    |
    v
Resources Created
    |
    v
Application Deployed
```

This can shorten the time between an infrastructure request and an environment being ready for development or testing.

sections.title: Automation
sections.content:
Cloud resources can be managed programmatically through APIs, CLI tools, SDKs, and infrastructure-as-code technologies.

This allows teams to define infrastructure in a repeatable way rather than manually configuring every environment.

```text
Infrastructure Code
       |
       v
Provisioning Tool
       |
       v
AWS APIs
       |
       v
Cloud Resources
```

Automation can reduce configuration drift and make infrastructure changes easier to review, reproduce, and integrate with CI/CD processes.

sections.title: Scalability and Elasticity
sections.content:
Cloud platforms provide services that can help applications handle changes in workload.

For example, an application can use load balancing and Auto Scaling to add or remove compute capacity based on demand.

```text
Normal Traffic
     |
     v
[EC2] [EC2]

Traffic Increases
     |
     v
[EC2] [EC2] [EC2] [EC2]

Traffic Decreases
     |
     v
[EC2] [EC2]
```

This can improve operational flexibility, but the application must be designed to scale correctly. A cloud provider cannot automatically make a poorly designed application horizontally scalable.

sections.title: Managed Services
sections.content:
Cloud providers offer managed services that remove some infrastructure administration from application teams.

For example, Amazon RDS can handle significant portions of the infrastructure involved in operating a relational database, allowing the team to focus more on database usage and application requirements.

Other managed services cover areas such as storage, messaging, monitoring, caching, analytics, and application integration.

```text
Without Managed Service
Application Team
      |
      +-- Server
      +-- OS
      +-- Database Software
      +-- Patching
      +-- Maintenance

With Managed Database Service
Application Team
      |
      +-- Database Configuration
      +-- Data
      +-- Application Integration
      |
      v
Managed Database Service
```

Managed services reduce operational responsibility, although customers still have configuration, security, data, and application responsibilities.

sections.title: Global Deployment
sections.content:
Cloud providers operate infrastructure in multiple geographic locations, allowing organizations to deploy workloads closer to their users or into multiple locations for availability and disaster-recovery requirements.

AWS provides Regions and Availability Zones that can be used to design geographically distributed architectures.

```text
                    Users
                      |
          +-----------+-----------+
          |                       |
          v                       v
      AWS Region A            AWS Region B
          |                       |
      Application             Application
          |                       |
       Database                Database
```

The appropriate design depends on application requirements such as latency, availability, data residency, disaster recovery, and operational complexity.

sections.title: Monitoring and Visibility
sections.content:
Cloud platforms provide monitoring and logging capabilities that can help teams understand the health and behavior of their workloads.

On AWS, Amazon CloudWatch can be used for metrics, logs, alarms, and other operational monitoring capabilities.

```text
Application / Infrastructure
            |
            v
       Metrics / Logs
            |
            v
        Monitoring
            |
       +----+----+
       |         |
       v         v
    Dashboard   Alarm
                 |
                 v
              Response
```

Monitoring allows teams to detect performance issues, capacity problems, failures, and unusual behavior more quickly.

sections.title: Operational Efficiency
sections.content:
Cloud computing can improve operational efficiency by reducing repetitive infrastructure tasks and allowing teams to standardize processes.

For example, an organization can use infrastructure-as-code, automated deployments, centralized logging, monitoring, and managed services as part of a repeatable operating model.

The benefit comes from combining cloud capabilities with good engineering practices.

```text
Cloud Services
      +
Automation
      +
Monitoring
      +
Standardization
      +
Managed Services
      |
      v
Improved Operational Efficiency
```

Cloud adoption should therefore be evaluated based on the operational model it enables, not simply on whether the application is running on cloud infrastructure.

topics.shortDescription: Learn how cloud computing can improve provisioning, automation, scalability, monitoring, global deployment, and day-to-day infrastructure operations.

topics.title: Cloud Provider Limitations
topics.description: Understand the practical limitations and trade-offs of using a cloud provider, including vendor dependency, service limits, outages, cost management, portability, and operational complexity.

sections.title: What Cloud Provider Limitations Mean
sections.content:
Cloud computing provides significant flexibility, but it does not remove every infrastructure or operational challenge. Cloud providers have service limits, pricing models, regional availability differences, dependencies, and platform-specific behaviors that architects need to consider.

A good cloud design considers both the capabilities and the limitations of the chosen services.

```text
Cloud Service
     |
     +-- Service Limits
     +-- Availability
     +-- Cost
     +-- Provider Dependency
     +-- Performance Constraints
     +-- Configuration Requirements
     |
     v
Application Architecture
```

Understanding these limitations early helps prevent architectural decisions that become difficult or expensive to change later.

sections.title: Service Quotas and Limits
sections.content:
AWS services have quotas that restrict how many resources can be created or how much capacity can be consumed. Some quotas are adjustable, while others are fixed for a particular service or resource.

For example, an account or Region can have limits on the number of certain resources, API request rates, or other service-specific capacities.

These limits matter when an application grows or when infrastructure is deployed automatically.

```text
Application Growth
       |
       v
More Resources / API Requests
       |
       v
AWS Service Quota
       |
   +---+---+
   |       |
 Within   Exceeded
 Limit      |
   |        v
   v     Request Increase /
Continue  Architecture Change
```

Production systems should identify important quotas before reaching them and monitor usage where appropriate.

sections.title: Vendor Dependency
sections.content:
Using cloud services can create a dependency on the provider's APIs, services, operating model, and pricing structure.

For example, an application designed heavily around AWS-specific services may require significant changes if the organization later wants to move the workload to another cloud provider.

This is commonly called vendor lock-in or vendor dependency.

```text
Application
    |
    +---- AWS-specific Services
    |           |
    |           v
    |       Provider APIs
    |
    v
Migration to Another Provider
           |
           v
      Potential Rework
```

Vendor dependency is not automatically a problem. Provider-specific services can provide useful capabilities and reduce operational work. The important point is to understand the trade-off between using native capabilities and maintaining portability.

sections.title: Cloud Outages and Availability
sections.content:
Moving an application to the cloud does not mean that the application can never experience an outage. Cloud services and infrastructure can experience failures, and applications can also fail because of incorrect configuration or application-level problems.

High availability therefore has to be designed into the architecture.

```text
                    Application
                         |
             +-----------+-----------+
             |                       |
             v                       v
       Availability Zone A    Availability Zone B
             |                       |
             v                       v
          Resources               Resources
```

For critical workloads, architects should consider redundancy, health checks, backups, recovery procedures, and appropriate disaster-recovery strategies.

sections.title: Cost Complexity
sections.content:
Cloud pricing can be flexible, but it can also become difficult to predict when an application uses many services or experiences changing traffic.

Costs can come from compute, storage, database usage, requests, data transfer, logging, monitoring, and other service-specific consumption.

```text
Cloud Bill
   |
   +-- Compute
   +-- Storage
   +-- Database
   +-- Requests
   +-- Data Transfer
   +-- Monitoring
   +-- Other Services
```

A resource that is inexpensive when used occasionally can become significant at high scale. Cost monitoring, budgets, tagging, right-sizing, and regular usage reviews can help organizations understand and control spending.

sections.title: Portability Considerations
sections.content:
Portability refers to how easily an application or workload can be moved between environments.

Applications using standard technologies may be easier to move, while applications that depend heavily on provider-specific APIs and services may require more changes.

```text
Portable Architecture
Application
    |
Standard Interfaces
    |
+---------+---------+
|                   |
AWS               Other Cloud


Provider-Specific Architecture
Application
    |
AWS-specific APIs
    |
AWS Services
```

Portability should be considered when it is an actual business requirement. Introducing abstractions solely for theoretical portability can also increase application complexity.

topics.shortDescription: Understand the important limitations and trade-offs of cloud providers, including quotas, outages, cost complexity, vendor dependency, and portability.

topics.title: Data Security
topics.description: Understand how to protect data in cloud environments through access control, encryption, backups, data classification, key management, and secure data handling.

sections.title: What Data Security Means
sections.content:
Data security is the practice of protecting data from unauthorized access, modification, disclosure, loss, or destruction.

In a cloud environment, data can exist in databases, object storage, block storage, backups, logs, and data transfers between services.

```text
                 Data
                   |
       +-----------+-----------+
       |           |           |
       v           v           v
   Database      Storage     Backup
       |           |           |
       +-----------+-----------+
                   |
                   v
              Security Controls
```

A secure design considers who can access the data, how data is protected while stored and transmitted, how keys are managed, and how data can be recovered after accidental deletion or failure.

sections.title: Data Classification
sections.content:
Data classification means identifying how sensitive different types of data are and applying appropriate controls.

Not every piece of data requires the same level of protection. Public application content may have different requirements from customer records, credentials, financial information, or confidential business data.

```text
Data
 |
 +-- Public
 |
 +-- Internal
 |
 +-- Confidential
 |
 +-- Highly Sensitive
```

Classification helps teams decide where data should be stored, who should access it, whether encryption is required, how long it should be retained, and how it should be handled during backups and transfers.

sections.title: Encryption at Rest
sections.content:
Encryption at rest protects stored data by encrypting it while it resides on storage systems.

AWS services can provide encryption capabilities for databases, storage, backups, and other resources. AWS Key Management Service (KMS) can be used to create and manage cryptographic keys for supported services and applications.

```text
Application
    |
    v
Encrypted Storage
    |
    v
Data at Rest

        +
        |
        v
     KMS / Keys
```

Encryption at rest reduces the impact of unauthorized access to the underlying stored data, but encryption does not replace access control. An authorized application can still access decrypted data.

sections.title: Encryption in Transit
sections.content:
Encryption in transit protects data while it is moving between systems.

For web applications, HTTPS using TLS is commonly used to protect communication between clients and application endpoints.

```text
Client
  |
  | Encrypted TLS Connection
  v
Load Balancer / API
  |
  | Encrypted Connection
  v
Application
  |
  | Encrypted Connection
  v
Database / Service
```

Encryption should be considered for communication between users, application components, databases, APIs, and other services whenever sensitive information is transmitted.

sections.title: Access Control for Data
sections.content:
Data should only be accessible to identities that require it. In AWS, IAM policies, resource policies, security controls, and service-specific permissions can be used to control access.

A common principle is least privilege: give an identity only the permissions required to perform its task.

```text
User / Application
       |
       v
Identity
       |
       v
Permission Policy
       |
   +---+---+
   |       |
 Allow    Deny
   |       |
   v       v
 Data     Block
```

Access should also be reviewed regularly because permissions that were appropriate during development may become excessive in production.

sections.title: Backup and Recovery
sections.content:
Protecting data also means preparing for accidental deletion, corruption, application errors, and infrastructure failures.

Backups should be designed according to recovery requirements rather than simply enabled without testing.

```text
Production Data
      |
      v
    Backup
      |
      v
Recovery Storage
      |
      v
Restore Test
      |
      v
Recovered Data
```

A backup strategy should consider backup frequency, retention, access protection, encryption, recovery time, recovery point requirements, and whether restoration has actually been tested.

sections.title: Data Security Best Practices
sections.content:
A practical cloud data-security approach includes:

- Classify sensitive data.
- Apply least-privilege access.
- Encrypt sensitive data at rest.
- Protect data in transit.
- Manage encryption keys securely.
- Avoid storing credentials directly in application source code.
- Protect and test backups.
- Monitor access to sensitive resources.
- Define appropriate retention and deletion policies.
- Review permissions and security configuration regularly.

Data security works as a collection of controls. Encryption alone is not sufficient if an unauthorized identity can access the application or storage resource.

topics.shortDescription: Learn how to protect cloud data using classification, access control, encryption, backups, key management, and secure data-handling practices.

topics.title: Network Security
topics.description: Understand how network security protects cloud workloads through network isolation, routing controls, security groups, network ACLs, private connectivity, and controlled internet access.

sections.title: What Network Security Means
sections.content:
Network security protects systems and data from unauthorized network access and unwanted traffic.

In AWS, network security is closely connected with VPC design, subnets, routing, security groups, network ACLs, gateways, and other networking services.

```text
Internet
   |
   v
Internet-facing Component
   |
   v
Public Subnet
   |
   v
Private Application Subnet
   |
   v
Private Database Subnet
```

The goal is to expose only the resources that need to be reachable and restrict communication between components according to the application's requirements.

sections.title: Network Isolation
sections.content:
Network isolation separates workloads into different network boundaries so that not every component can communicate freely with every other component.

An AWS VPC can contain multiple subnets and routing configurations that help create these boundaries.

```text
                 VPC
                  |
       +----------+----------+
       |          |          |
       v          v          v
    Public     Private     Private
    Subnet     App         Database
                 Subnet      Subnet
```

For example, a database usually does not need to accept direct connections from the public internet. Keeping it in a private network location reduces its exposure.

sections.title: Security Groups
sections.content:
Security groups act as virtual firewalls associated with supported AWS resources. They control network traffic according to configured rules.

For example, a web application might allow HTTPS traffic from users while allowing database traffic only from the application tier.

```text
Internet
   |
 HTTPS
   v
[Web Tier]
   |
 DB Port
   v
[Database]

Security Group Rules
Web: HTTPS allowed
DB: Database port allowed from Web SG
```

Using references between security groups can help express application-tier relationships without allowing broad network access.

sections.title: Network ACLs
sections.content:
Network Access Control Lists (network ACLs) provide subnet-level traffic controls in a VPC.

They operate at a different level from security groups and can provide an additional network-control layer.

```text
VPC
 |
 +-- Subnet
       |
       +-- Network ACL
              |
              +-- Allow / Deny Rules
              |
              v
          Resources
```

Because network ACLs are stateless, return traffic must be considered separately in the rules. This differs from the stateful behavior commonly associated with security groups.

sections.title: Public vs Private Resources
sections.content:
A secure architecture should distinguish between resources that need public connectivity and resources that can remain private.

A common application design places only the required entry points in a public-facing subnet while keeping application and database resources private.

```text
Internet
   |
   v
Public Subnet
   |
   v
Load Balancer
   |
   v
Private Subnet
   |
   +---- Application
   |
   v
Private Database Subnet
   |
   +---- Database
```

Private resources can still reach required external services through controlled mechanisms such as NAT when appropriate, without being directly reachable from the public internet.

sections.title: Network Security Monitoring
sections.content:
Network security also requires visibility into traffic and configuration.

Depending on the architecture, teams can use AWS logging and monitoring capabilities to investigate network behavior and detect unexpected access patterns.

```text
Network Traffic
      |
      v
Logs / Flow Information
      |
      v
Monitoring / Analysis
      |
      v
Security Investigation
```

Monitoring is particularly useful when troubleshooting unexpected connections, blocked traffic, unusual traffic volume, or possible security incidents.

sections.title: Network Security Design Principles
sections.content:
Important network-security principles include:

- Minimize public exposure.
- Separate application tiers where appropriate.
- Allow only required ports and protocols.
- Use least-privilege network rules.
- Keep sensitive services private when public access is unnecessary.
- Monitor network behavior.
- Review routing and firewall rules regularly.
- Design for failure without opening unnecessary access.

Network security should be designed together with application architecture because network boundaries determine how application components can communicate.

topics.shortDescription: Learn how AWS network controls protect workloads through VPC isolation, security groups, network ACLs, private subnets, and traffic monitoring.

topics.title: Application Security
topics.description: Understand application security in cloud environments, including identity management, secure configuration, secrets protection, input validation, dependency security, logging, and secure application architecture.

sections.title: What Application Security Means
sections.content:
Application security is the practice of protecting an application from vulnerabilities, unauthorized access, data exposure, and misuse.

Cloud infrastructure can provide strong security controls, but the application itself still needs secure code, authentication, authorization, input validation, dependency management, and secure configuration.

```text
                Application Security
                        |
       +----------------+----------------+
       |                |                |
       v                v                v
 Authentication   Authorization      Secure Code
       |                |                |
       +----------------+----------------+
                        |
                        v
                 Protected Application
```

Running an application on AWS does not automatically make the application secure. Security responsibilities remain at the application level.

sections.title: Authentication and Authorization
sections.content:
Authentication determines who or what is requesting access. Authorization determines what that identity is allowed to do.

These concepts should be kept separate.

```text
Request
  |
  v
Authentication
  |
  | Valid identity?
  v
Authorization
  |
  | Allowed action?
  v
Application Resource
```

For example, a user may be authenticated successfully but still be unauthorized to access an administrator-only endpoint.

Cloud applications should use appropriate identity mechanisms and avoid implementing access control through insecure hard-coded rules.

sections.title: Secrets Management
sections.content:
Applications often require sensitive values such as database passwords, API keys, tokens, and encryption-related configuration.

These values should not be stored directly in source code or committed to source-control repositories.

AWS services such as AWS Secrets Manager can be used to store and retrieve application secrets securely.

```text
Application
    |
    | Request Secret
    v
Secrets Manager
    |
    v
Secret Value
```

Access to secrets should itself be controlled using appropriate permissions, and secrets should be rotated when required.

sections.title: Input Validation
sections.content:
Applications should treat external input as untrusted data.

Input can come from web requests, APIs, files, message queues, users, or other services. Validation helps ensure that the application accepts data in the expected format and rejects invalid or dangerous input.

```text
External Input
      |
      v
Validation
      |
   +--+--+
   |     |
 Valid  Invalid
   |     |
   v     v
Process  Reject
```

Input validation should be combined with secure coding practices such as parameterized database queries, output encoding where appropriate, and safe handling of uploaded files.

sections.title: Dependency and Patch Management
sections.content:
Applications depend on frameworks, libraries, operating systems, container images, and other components. Vulnerabilities in these dependencies can create security risks even when the application's own code appears correct.

A secure development process should track dependencies and apply security updates according to risk and operational requirements.

```text
Application
   |
   +-- Framework
   +-- Libraries
   +-- Runtime
   +-- Container Image
   |
   v
Security Updates / Vulnerability Management
```

Updates should be tested before production deployment, especially for critical applications.

sections.title: Logging and Security Monitoring
sections.content:
Applications should generate useful logs for operational and security investigation without exposing sensitive information.

Security-relevant events can include authentication failures, authorization failures, administrative actions, unexpected configuration changes, and unusual application behavior.

```text
Application Events
       |
       v
      Logs
       |
       v
Monitoring / Analysis
       |
       v
Alert / Investigation
```

Logs should be protected from unauthorized modification and access. Sensitive credentials and unnecessary personal or confidential information should not be written into application logs.

sections.title: Secure Application Architecture
sections.content:
Application security should be built into the architecture rather than added at the end.

A secure cloud application commonly combines identity controls, network isolation, encryption, secrets management, secure coding, monitoring, and controlled deployment processes.

```text
                 Application
                      |
      +---------------+---------------+
      |               |               |
      v               v               v
 Identity          Network         Data Security
      |               |               |
      +---------------+---------------+
                      |
                      v
                 Monitoring
```

Security is therefore a layered process. A weakness in one layer should not automatically expose the entire application.

topics.shortDescription: Learn the application-level security practices needed to protect cloud workloads, including authentication, authorization, secrets, secure coding, and monitoring.

topics.title: Compliance
topics.description: Understand cloud compliance, why organizations have regulatory and contractual requirements, and how AWS security, logging, data protection, and governance capabilities support compliance programs.

sections.title: What Cloud Compliance Means
sections.content:
Cloud compliance means operating systems and handling data according to applicable laws, regulations, industry standards, contractual requirements, and internal policies.

Compliance requirements vary depending on factors such as industry, geography, type of data, and business activities.

```text
Business
   |
   +-- Laws / Regulations
   +-- Industry Standards
   +-- Contracts
   +-- Internal Policies
   |
   v
Compliance Requirements
   |
   v
Cloud Architecture + Operations
```

Compliance is not a single AWS feature. It requires appropriate architecture, processes, controls, documentation, monitoring, and evidence.

sections.title: Why Compliance Matters
sections.content:
Organizations may have legal, regulatory, contractual, or internal requirements for protecting information and operating systems.

For example, a company handling sensitive customer information may need controls around access, encryption, auditing, retention, and incident response.

Compliance requirements can influence architecture decisions such as where data is stored, who can access it, how long it is retained, and what activity must be logged.

```text
Compliance Requirement
          |
          v
Security / Operational Control
          |
          v
AWS Configuration
          |
          v
Evidence and Monitoring
```

Meeting a compliance requirement generally involves demonstrating that required controls are implemented and operating effectively.

sections.title: AWS and Shared Compliance Responsibility
sections.content:
AWS provides infrastructure and services that can support organizations with their compliance obligations, but using AWS does not automatically make a workload compliant.

AWS is responsible for compliance aspects of the underlying cloud infrastructure according to its responsibilities, while customers remain responsible for compliance controls applicable to their workloads.

```text
AWS Responsibilities
        |
        +-- Cloud Infrastructure
        +-- Physical Security
        +-- Underlying Services

Customer Responsibilities
        |
        +-- Application
        +-- Data
        +-- Access Controls
        +-- Configuration
        +-- Workload-specific Controls
```

The exact responsibilities depend on the AWS service and the organization's requirements.

sections.title: Data Residency and Location
sections.content:
Some organizations have requirements about where certain data can be stored or processed.

AWS Regions allow workloads and data to be deployed in specific geographic locations, but selecting a Region should be based on the actual legal, regulatory, business, and technical requirements.

```text
Business Requirement
        |
        v
Data Location Requirement
        |
        v
AWS Region Selection
        |
        v
Storage / Processing Architecture
```

Data residency should be reviewed carefully because applications can also move or copy data through backups, replication, logs, integrations, and other services.

sections.title: Audit Logging and Evidence
sections.content:
Compliance programs often require evidence showing that security and operational controls are functioning.

Cloud environments can generate logs and audit records that help organizations investigate activity and demonstrate how resources were used or changed.

For example, AWS CloudTrail records AWS API activity and can support auditing of actions performed against AWS resources.

```text
AWS Activity
     |
     v
Audit Records
     |
     v
Storage / Monitoring
     |
     v
Compliance Evidence
```

Audit data should itself be protected because unauthorized modification or deletion of logs can reduce their value during an investigation.

sections.title: Security Controls for Compliance
sections.content:
Compliance requirements often translate into concrete technical controls.

Examples include:

- Identity and access management.
- Encryption.
- Network isolation.
- Logging and auditing.
- Backup and recovery.
- Vulnerability management.
- Data retention and deletion.
- Monitoring and alerting.
- Change management.

```text
Compliance Requirement
          |
          v
       Control
          |
          v
AWS Service / Configuration
          |
          v
Monitoring + Evidence
```

The control should be mapped to the requirement rather than enabling security features without understanding what they are intended to achieve.

sections.title: Compliance Is an Ongoing Process
sections.content:
Compliance is not something that is completed once and then forgotten. Cloud environments change continuously as applications, permissions, infrastructure, and data change.

A compliant environment therefore needs ongoing monitoring, reviews, testing, documentation, and evidence collection.

```text
Implement Controls
       |
       v
Monitor
       |
       v
Review
       |
       v
Test / Audit
       |
       v
Improve Controls
       |
       +------> Repeat
```

Automation can help identify configuration changes and enforce standards consistently, but organizations still need appropriate governance and human oversight.

topics.shortDescription: Learn the fundamentals of cloud compliance and how security controls, data location, auditing, and governance support regulatory and business requirements.

topics.title: The AWS Sandbox
topics.description: Understand the AWS sandbox concept, why isolated environments are useful for learning and experimentation, and how to work safely with AWS resources.

sections.title: What Is an AWS Sandbox?
sections.content:
An AWS sandbox is an isolated environment where developers, engineers, students, or teams can experiment with AWS services without affecting production workloads.

A sandbox can be used to create resources, test configurations, learn how AWS services behave, and validate ideas before introducing changes into shared or production environments.

```text
                    AWS Account / Environment
                              |
              +---------------+---------------+
              |               |               |
              v               v               v
          Development       Sandbox       Production
              |               |               |
              v               v               v
           Testing       Experiments       Live Users
```

The exact isolation model depends on how the organization structures its AWS accounts, environments, networking, and permissions.

sections.title: Why Use a Sandbox?
sections.content:
A sandbox provides a safer place to learn and experiment with cloud services.

Typical uses include:

- Learning a new AWS service.
- Testing infrastructure configurations.
- Trying application deployment approaches.
- Validating IAM policies.
- Experimenting with networking.
- Testing automation scripts.
- Evaluating an architecture before implementation.

For example, an engineer learning Amazon VPC can create a small network, test routing and security rules, and observe the behavior without modifying the production network.

sections.title: Sandbox vs Production
sections.content:
A sandbox should have clear boundaries from production. The purpose is to allow experimentation while reducing the possibility that an experiment affects real users or business data.

```text
Sandbox
  |
  +-- Test Resources
  +-- Sample Data
  +-- Experiments
  +-- Temporary Configuration

Production
  |
  +-- Live Application
  +-- Real Data
  +-- Business Workloads
  +-- Controlled Changes
```

Production environments normally require stricter access controls, change management, monitoring, backup policies, and operational procedures.

sections.title: Sandbox Safety
sections.content:
A sandbox reduces risk, but it should still be managed carefully. AWS resources can consume billable resources, expose data, or create security risks if they are configured incorrectly.

Useful practices include:

- Use appropriate IAM permissions.
- Avoid using production credentials in experiments.
- Use test or synthetic data where possible.
- Monitor resource usage and costs.
- Delete resources that are no longer required.
- Avoid making unnecessary resources publicly accessible.
- Keep experiments isolated from production networks and data.

A sandbox should make experimentation safer, not encourage uncontrolled access or resource creation.

topics.shortDescription: Learn how AWS sandbox environments support safe experimentation, learning, testing, and architecture validation.

topics.title: Identify The Problem First
topics.description: Learn why AWS architecture decisions should begin with the business and technical problem rather than starting with a specific AWS service.

sections.title: Start With the Problem
sections.content:
A common mistake when learning or designing on AWS is starting with a service and then trying to find a problem for it to solve.

A better approach is to identify the actual requirement first and then select the AWS capability that addresses it.

```text
Business / Technical Problem
            |
            v
        Requirements
            |
            v
       Constraints
            |
            v
    Architecture Options
            |
            v
      AWS Services
```

For example, if an application is slow because database queries are taking too long, the solution may involve query optimization, indexing, caching, database scaling, or architectural changes. Simply adding another AWS service without understanding the bottleneck may not solve the problem.

sections.title: Define the Requirements
sections.content:
Before selecting an AWS service, identify what the system actually needs.

Important requirements can include:

- Expected traffic.
- Latency requirements.
- Availability requirements.
- Data volume.
- Security requirements.
- Recovery objectives.
- Compliance requirements.
- Budget constraints.
- Operational capabilities of the team.

```text
Requirements
   |
   +-- Performance
   +-- Availability
   +-- Security
   +-- Cost
   +-- Operations
   +-- Scalability
   +-- Recovery
```

These requirements provide the context needed to evaluate different AWS services and architectural approaches.

sections.title: Understand Constraints
sections.content:
Real-world architecture decisions are made within constraints. A technically possible design may not be appropriate if it exceeds the budget, requires skills the team does not have, or conflicts with regulatory requirements.

For example, an organization may have an existing database that cannot immediately be replaced. In that case, migration may need to happen in stages rather than through a complete redesign.

```text
Ideal Architecture
       |
       v
Business Constraints
       |
       +-- Budget
       +-- Skills
       +-- Existing Systems
       +-- Compliance
       +-- Timeline
       |
       v
Practical Architecture
```

Good architecture balances technical capabilities with real business constraints.

sections.title: Avoid Service-First Thinking
sections.content:
AWS provides hundreds of services, and it is easy to assume that every problem should be solved by adding another service.

Service-first thinking can lead to unnecessary complexity.

Instead of asking, "Which AWS service should I use?", start with questions such as:

- What problem are we trying to solve?
- What is causing the current problem?
- What does the application need to do?
