- What constraints must the solution satisfy?
- What is the simplest architecture that meets those requirements?

Only after answering these questions should AWS services be evaluated.

sections.title: Problem to Architecture
sections.content:
A useful architecture process is to progressively translate the problem into technical decisions.

```text
Problem
  |
  v
Requirements
  |
  v
Workload Characteristics
  |
  v
Architecture Pattern
  |
  v
AWS Services
  |
  v
Implementation
  |
  v
Measure and Improve
```

This approach keeps the architecture connected to the original business or technical goal and makes trade-offs easier to explain.

topics.shortDescription: Learn how to start AWS architecture decisions from the actual problem, requirements, and constraints instead of choosing services first.

topics.title: Migrating Applications
topics.description: Understand the main considerations involved in moving applications to AWS, including assessment, dependencies, migration strategies, data movement, testing, and production cutover.

sections.title: What Application Migration Means
sections.content:
Application migration is the process of moving an application and its required infrastructure, data, and dependencies from one environment to another.

The source environment might be a physical data center, an existing hosting provider, or another cloud platform.

Moving an application to AWS does not necessarily mean rewriting it. The migration approach depends on the application's architecture, business requirements, technical constraints, and desired outcome.

```text
Existing Environment
       |
       | Assessment
       v
Migration Strategy
       |
       v
AWS Target Architecture
       |
       v
Migration + Testing
       |
       v
Production Cutover
```

The objective is to move the workload safely while maintaining required functionality, security, performance, and availability.

sections.title: Assess the Application
sections.content:
Before migrating an application, understand how it currently works.

The assessment should identify:

- Application servers.
- Operating systems.
- Databases.
- Storage requirements.
- Network dependencies.
- External APIs.
- Authentication systems.
- Scheduled jobs.
- Performance characteristics.
- Data sensitivity.

```text
Application
    |
    +-- Compute
    +-- Database
    +-- Storage
    +-- Network
    +-- Authentication
    +-- External Services
    +-- Scheduled Jobs
```

Understanding these dependencies reduces the risk of discovering critical requirements after the migration has already started.

sections.title: Choose a Migration Strategy
sections.content:
Different applications require different migration strategies. Common approaches include rehosting, replatforming, refactoring, repurchasing, retiring, and retaining.

**Rehosting** moves the application with minimal changes.

**Replatforming** makes selected changes to take advantage of cloud capabilities while keeping most of the application architecture.

**Refactoring** significantly changes the architecture to take advantage of cloud-native capabilities.

**Repurchasing** replaces an existing application or platform with another product.

**Retiring** removes workloads that are no longer needed.

**Retaining** keeps a workload in its current environment when migration is not currently appropriate.

The strategy should be selected based on the desired outcome rather than applying the same strategy to every application.

sections.title: Plan Data Migration
sections.content:
Application migration often requires moving databases, files, objects, and other data.

The data migration approach depends on data size, network bandwidth, database technology, acceptable downtime, consistency requirements, and recovery needs.

```text
Source Data
    |
    +-- Initial Transfer
    |
    v
AWS Target
    ^
    |
    +-- Ongoing Synchronization
    |
    v
Final Cutover
```

For large or continuously changing datasets, the migration may require an initial copy followed by synchronization before the final application cutover.

sections.title: Test the Migrated Application
sections.content:
A migrated application should be tested before production traffic is moved to AWS.

Testing should cover:

- Application functionality.
- Database connectivity.
- External integrations.
- Authentication and authorization.
- Network connectivity.
- Performance.
- Data integrity.
- Monitoring and logging.
- Backup and recovery.

The objective is to confirm that the AWS environment behaves correctly for real application workflows, not simply that the application process starts successfully.

sections.title: Production Cutover
sections.content:
Production cutover is the point where users are directed to the AWS environment.

A cutover plan should define the migration sequence, validation steps, communication process, monitoring approach, and rollback procedure.

```text
Existing Production
        |
        v
Final Data Synchronization
        |
        v
AWS Environment Validation
        |
        v
Traffic / DNS Change
        |
        v
AWS Production
        |
        v
Monitor Closely
```

After cutover, teams should monitor application errors, latency, resource utilization, database behavior, and business transactions.

topics.shortDescription: Learn how to assess, plan, test, and safely migrate applications and their dependencies to AWS.

topics.title: Well-Architected Tool
topics.description: Understand the AWS Well-Architected Tool and how it can be used to review workloads, identify architectural risks, document decisions, and track improvements.

sections.title: What Is the AWS Well-Architected Tool?
sections.content:
The AWS Well-Architected Tool is an AWS service that helps teams review workloads against the AWS Well-Architected Framework.

It provides a structured way to document a workload, answer questions related to architectural practices, identify risks, and track improvement actions.

```text
AWS Workload
     |
     v
Well-Architected Tool
     |
     +-- Review Questions
     +-- Architectural Risks
     +-- Improvement Actions
     +-- Milestones / Progress
     |
     v
Improved Architecture
```

The tool is useful during architecture reviews because it provides a repeatable process rather than relying only on informal discussions.

sections.title: Create a Workload Review
sections.content:
A workload review starts by defining the workload being evaluated and providing relevant information about its architecture and operational context.

The review then walks through questions associated with the Well-Architected Framework pillars.

```text
Define Workload
      |
      v
Select / Review Pillars
      |
      v
Answer Questions
      |
      v
Identify Risks
      |
      v
Plan Improvements
```

The quality of the review depends on the accuracy of the information provided. The tool does not replace architectural judgment; it helps structure that judgment.

sections.title: Identify High-Risk Areas
sections.content:
A Well-Architected review can highlight areas where the workload does not follow recommended practices or where additional attention may be needed.

For example, a review may reveal that a workload has insufficient backup testing, overly broad permissions, limited monitoring, or resources that are not aligned with expected demand.

```text
Architecture Review
       |
       v
Questions
       |
       v
Potential Risks
       |
       +-- Security
       +-- Reliability
       +-- Performance
       +-- Operations
       +-- Cost
       +-- Sustainability
```

Identifying a risk does not automatically mean that a particular remediation must be implemented. The team should evaluate the risk against workload requirements and constraints.

sections.title: Improvement Plans
sections.content:
After identifying architectural risks, teams can create improvement actions and track progress toward addressing them.

An improvement plan should explain what needs to change, why the change matters, who owns it, and how completion will be verified.

```text
Risk Identified
      |
      v
Improvement Action
      |
      v
Owner + Priority
      |
      v
Implementation
      |
      v
Validation
      |
      v
Review Again
```

This turns an architecture review from a static assessment into an ongoing improvement process.

sections.title: When to Use the Tool
sections.content:
The Well-Architected Tool can be useful at different stages of a workload's lifecycle.

It can be used:

- During initial architecture design.
- Before production launch.
- During migration to AWS.
- After significant architecture changes.
- During periodic operational reviews.
- When investigating architectural risks.
- When planning modernization work.

```text
Design
  |
  v
Review
  |
  v
Build
  |
  v
Operate
  |
  v
Re-Review
```

Using the tool periodically helps teams revisit architectural assumptions as the workload evolves.

sections.title: Tool vs Architectural Judgment
sections.content:
The Well-Architected Tool provides structure and guidance, but it does not automatically design the correct architecture for every workload.

Architects still need to understand the application's requirements, constraints, dependencies, risks, and trade-offs.

```text
Well-Architected Tool
          +
Workload Knowledge
          +
Engineering Judgment
          |
          v
Architecture Decisions
```

A recommendation should therefore be evaluated in context. The objective is to make informed decisions that meet the workload's requirements, not simply to complete every checklist item without understanding why it matters.

topics.title: Monitoring
topics.description: Monitoring answers: - Is the system healthy?

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Monitoring answers:
- Is the system healthy?
- Is performance degrading?
- Is capacity sufficient?
- Did a deployment cause a problem?
- Is a dependency failing?
- Is cost increasing unexpectedly?

A useful monitoring model is:

```
Metrics -> detect
Logs -> investigate
Traces -> follow requests across services
Alerts -> notify
Dashboards -> understand trends
```

sections.title: Example
sections.content: The platform tracks latency, errors, capacity, database health, and application logs, with alarms connected to operational responses.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Use Monitoring to make production behavior measurable and diagnosable. Define the signal, threshold, owner, and response before enabling it so the resulting telemetry leads to action.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interview focus: Explain which signal Monitoring provides, where that signal comes from, how you would detect a real incident, and how you would avoid alerting on normal noise. Distinguish symptoms from root-cause evidence.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Common mistakes: collecting telemetry without an operational question, creating alerts for every metric, or relying on a single signal to diagnose an incident. Good observability connects signals to decisions.

The source introduces the Twelve-Factor methodology. The ideas are useful for
cloud-native application design.

Factor 1 — Codebase
One tracked codebase can support many deploys.

Factor 2 — Dependencies
Explicitly declare and isolate dependencies.

Factor 3 — Config
Store environment-specific configuration outside application code.

Factor 4 — Backing services
Treat databases, queues, storage, and other services as attached resources.

Factor 5 — Build, release, run
Separate building the application from releasing and executing it.

Factor 6 — Processes
Run applications as stateless processes where appropriate.

Factor 7 — Port binding
Expose services through ports rather than relying on a preinstalled application
server.

Factor 8 — Concurrency
Scale through additional processes/instances rather than only increasing one
machine.

Factor 9 — Disposability
Design for fast startup and graceful shutdown.

Factor 10 — Dev/prod parity
Keep environments as similar as practical.

Factor 11 — Logs
Treat logs as event streams and centralize their handling.

Factor 12 — Admin processes
Run administrative tasks as controlled one-off processes.

topics.title: Deployment
topics.description: Putting every server in one Availability Zone.

sections.title: Detailed explanation
sections.content:
Pipeline:

```
Source
|
Build
|
Test
|
Security Validation
|
Staging
|
Approval
|
Production
|
Health Check
|
Controlled Traffic Shift
```

COMMON AWS MISTAKES

1. Putting every server in one Availability Zone.
2. Making databases publicly reachable without a compelling reason.
3. Using broad IAM permissions.
4. Storing access keys in application code.
5. Treating S3 like a traditional file system.
6. Using local instance storage as the only copy of critical data.
7. Assuming backups automatically mean disaster recovery is tested.
8. Ignoring data-transfer charges.
9. Selecting an instance by CPU count alone.
10. Creating alerts without defining response actions.
11. Using sticky sessions to hide a state-management problem.
12. Choosing Kubernetes without a real operational requirement.
13. Assuming serverless means zero operational responsibility.
14. Forgetting Region-specific service availability.
15. Treating an SLA as a guarantee for the entire application.
16. Scaling compute while ignoring the database bottleneck.
17. Creating a very large VPC CIDR without considering connected networks.
18. Allowing unrestricted inbound traffic for convenience.
19. Making manual production changes that are not captured in infrastructure code.
20. Failing to test restore and failover procedures.

sections.title: Example
sections.content: Application changes pass through version control, automated tests, and a controlled deployment process. If health checks fail, the rollout stops or rolls back according to the chosen strategy.

sections.title: Practical use
sections.content: Use Deployment when repeatability and controlled change matter. Keep infrastructure or deployment definitions versioned, reviewable, testable, and safe to roll back.

sections.title: Interview focus
sections.content: Interview focus: Explain what Deployment makes repeatable, how changes are reviewed and promoted, and what happens when a deployment partially fails. Mention drift, rollback, and the difference between desired state and runtime state where relevant.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Common mistakes: mixing manual production changes with automated deployments, storing secrets in templates or repositories, or assuming a successful deployment means the system is healthy. Test rollback and post-deployment verification.
